verse.text: Simeon Peter, a slave and apostle of Jesus Christ, to those who have been allotted a faith of equal standing with ours through the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ:
verse.note: The Greek text followed here has “Simeon,” the Semitic form of the name, which is used of Peter elsewhere only in Acts 15:14. Many manuscripts have the common Greek form “Simon,” which older English versions follow. Most editors judge “Simeon” original because scribes would more readily change the rare form to the familiar one.

The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master, not a hired servant. Most English versions soften it to “servant,” partly because of the associations of modern slavery. In the Septuagint “slave of the Lord” is also a title of honor for figures such as Moses and David, and both notes are probably heard here.

Greek has one word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice). Most translations have “righteousness” here. A number of scholars think the point in this verse is fairness: Christ shows no favoritism in giving later believers a faith of equal standing with that of the apostles, and they would translate “justice.”

note.term: our God and Savior Jesus Christ
note.traditional: our God and Savior Jesus Christ

verse.note: The Greek has one article governing both “God” and “Savior,” which most naturally makes both titles refer to Jesus Christ, just as “our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” does in verse 11. This is the majority view. The phrase can also be read as naming two persons, “our God, and the Savior Jesus Christ,” as verse 2 distinguishes God from Jesus.

verse.text: May grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.
His divine power has granted us everything needed for life and godliness, through the knowledge of the one who called us by his own glory and virtue.

note.traditional: excellence (of God, verse 3); virtue (of believers, verse 5)

verse.note: Many versions use two English words, “excellence” here and “virtue” in verse 5, or “goodness” in both. The Greek uses the same word in both places, the standard Greek term for moral excellence, and the echo seems deliberate: believers are to supply what the one who called them displays. Used of a deity the word could also suggest a display of divine power.

verse.text: Through these he has granted us his precious and very great promises, so that through them you may become sharers in the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world because of desire.
For this very reason, make every effort to supply your faith with virtue, virtue with knowledge,
knowledge with self-control, self-control with endurance, endurance with godliness,
godliness with brotherly affection, and brotherly affection with love.
For when these things are yours and are increasing, they make you neither idle nor unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.
For whoever lacks these things is blind, nearsighted, having forgotten the cleansing of their past sins.
Therefore, brothers and sisters, put all the more effort into making your calling and choosing sure; for if you do these things, you will never stumble.
verse.note: The traditional “calling and election” uses a word that now suggests voting. The Greek means a choice or selection, here God’s choosing of the readers, just as “calling” means God’s calling of them. To make it “sure” is to confirm it by the way of life described in verses 5 to 7.

verse.text: For in this way entry into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ will be richly supplied to you.
Therefore I intend to keep reminding you of these things, even though you know them and are firmly established in the truth you now have.
I consider it right, as long as I am in this tent, to stir you up with a reminder,
verse.note: This is the adjective usually rendered “righteous” or “just.” Here it stands in a common Greek idiom, “to consider it right,” meaning proper or fitting, where neither of those words is natural English. Nearly all translations render it “right.”

“Tent” is a figure for the mortal body as a temporary dwelling, an image familiar in both Jewish and Greek writing. Some translations replace it with “body.” Verse 14 mixes this image with that of taking off a garment, and “departure” in verse 15 translates the Greek word exodos, a common euphemism for death.

verse.text: since I know that I will soon put off my tent, as indeed our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me.
And I will make every effort so that after my departure you will be able at any time to call these things to mind.
For we were not following cleverly devised myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ; rather, we had been eyewitnesses of his majesty.
verse.note: The Greek word means arrival and presence, and was the regular term for the official visit of a king or emperor to a city. Early Christians used it for the future arrival of Jesus in glory. Most interpreters take that future coming to be meant here, with the transfiguration (verses 17 and 18) offered as a foretaste of it.

verse.text: For he received honor and glory from God the Father when a voice like this was carried to him by the Majestic Glory: “This is my Son, my Beloved, with whom I myself am well pleased.”

note.traditional: came (of the voice and of prophecy); moved (by the Holy Spirit)

verse.note: The same Greek verb, “carry” or “bring,” is used four times: of the voice carried to Jesus (verse 17) and from heaven (verse 18), of prophecy not carried by human will, and of the prophets carried along by the Spirit (verse 21). Most translations vary the English (“came,” “borne,” “moved”). The repetition is kept here because it links the heavenly voice and prophecy as having the same source.

verse.text: We ourselves heard this voice carried from heaven when we were with him on the holy mountain.
So we have the prophetic word made more sure. You do well to pay attention to it, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts,

note.traditional: a more sure word of prophecy

verse.note: The Greek says literally “we have the prophetic word more sure.” This can mean that what the apostles saw confirms the prophetic word, as rendered here and in many modern versions. It can also mean that the prophetic word is something even more sure than the eyewitness experience, or simply that it is “very sure.” Scholars are divided.

verse.text: knowing this first of all, that no prophecy of Scripture comes from one’s own interpretation,
verse.note: The Greek does not say whose interpretation is meant. On one reading, favored by many scholars because of verse 21, the point is that prophecy did not originate in the prophet’s own interpretation of things. On the other, which is the traditional one, it is that readers may not interpret prophecy as they please. The rendering leaves both open.

verse.text: for no prophecy was ever carried by human will; rather, carried along by the Holy Spirit, people spoke from God.
verse.note: Many later manuscripts read “holy people of God spoke” in place of “people spoke from God,” and the King James Version follows them. The two readings differ by only a few letters in Greek. Most editors judge “from God” to be original.

verse.text: But there were also false prophets among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you too, who will introduce destructive opinions, even denying the Master who bought them, and bringing swift destruction on themselves.
verse.note: The Greek word meant a chosen position, school of thought or faction, and had not yet acquired the later technical sense of “heresy” as officially condemned doctrine. Most versions keep “heresies”; some, like this one, use “opinions,” and “factions” is also possible. The phrase is literally “opinions of destruction,” echoing the “destruction” these teachers bring on themselves.

verse.text: And many will follow them in their debauchery, and because of them the way of truth will be slandered.
verse.note: In first-century Greek this verb covered abusive or defamatory speech against anyone or anything, not only against God. Modern English “blaspheme” is limited to irreverence toward God, so “slander” is used here and in verses 10–12 where the target is the Christian way or angelic beings. Several modern versions keep “blaspheme” or use “malign” or “revile” in these verses.

verse.text: In their greed they will make money out of you with fabricated words. The verdict against them from long ago is not idle, and their destruction is not asleep.
For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but sent them down to Tartarus in chains of gloom and handed them over to be kept for judgment;
verse.note: The Greek verb, found only here in the New Testament, means to consign to Tartarus, the name in Greek tradition for the deep place where rebellious divine beings were imprisoned; Jewish writers in Greek had already borrowed it. It is a different word from those usually rendered “hell” or “Hades,” so the name is kept. Some manuscripts read “pits of gloom” in place of “chains of gloom”; the two Greek words differ only slightly.

verse.text: and if he did not spare the ancient world, but protected Noah, a herald of righteousness, with seven others, when he brought a flood on a world of ungodly people;
and if he reduced the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes and condemned them to ruin, making them an example of what is coming for the ungodly;
and if he rescued righteous Lot, who was worn down by the debauched conduct of unprincipled people—
for that righteous man, living among them day after day, was tormenting his righteous soul over the lawless deeds he saw and heard—
then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trial and to keep the unrighteous under punishment for the day of judgment,
verse.note: The Greek word chiefly means a putting to the proof, an ordeal that tests faithfulness, and here it refers to the kind of hardship Noah and Lot lived through. Older versions have “temptations”; most modern versions likewise have “trial” or “trials” here.

The Greek participle is present tense and most naturally means the unrighteous are already being punished while held for the day of judgment, like the angels of verse 4. It can also be read as pointing forward: “to keep the unrighteous for the day of judgment, to be punished then.” Translations and commentators are divided.

verse.text: especially those who go after the flesh in defiling desire and despise authority. Reckless and arrogant, they do not tremble as they slander the glorious ones,
verse.note: The Greek is literally “glories.” Most interpreters take it as a term for angelic beings, as in the parallel at Jude 8, though it is disputed whether good or fallen angels are meant; a minority think of human authorities. “Them” in verse 11 most likely refers to these beings, though some refer it to the false teachers.

verse.text: whereas angels, though greater in strength and power, do not bring a slanderous judgment against them.
verse.note: Many manuscripts add “before the Lord” after these words, and some read “from the Lord.” The Greek text followed here has neither, and the evidence is closely balanced; many English versions include “before the Lord.”

verse.text: But these people, like unreasoning animals, creatures of instinct born to be caught and destroyed, slander what they do not understand, and in the destruction of those creatures they too will be destroyed,

note.term: in the destruction of those creatures
note.traditional: shall utterly perish in their own corruption

verse.note: The Greek says “in their destruction they too will be destroyed,” repeating one word-family three times in the verse. “Their” may refer to the animals (these people will die as animals die) or to the false teachers themselves, in which case the noun could mean their own moral corruption. The same Greek noun is rendered “corruption” in verse 19.

verse.text: suffering wrong as the wages of wrongdoing. They count it a pleasure to revel in the daytime. Stains and blemishes, they revel in their deceptions while they feast with you.

note.term: suffering wrong as the wages of wrongdoing

verse.note: The Greek plays on two related words: they are “wronged” as the pay for “wrongdoing,” meaning they are paid back in kind. “Wages” keeps the word’s ordinary sense of a worker’s pay and matches verse 15, where Balaam loves the same “wages.” Some manuscripts read “receiving” in place of “suffering wrong,” which is the reading behind the older English versions.

Some manuscripts read “love feasts” (the community’s shared meals) in place of “deceptions”; the two Greek words differ by two letters, and the parallel at Jude 12 has “love feasts.” The reading “deceptions” is usually judged original here, perhaps as a deliberate play on the other word.

verse.text: They have eyes full of adultery that never rest from sin; they lure unstable souls; they have hearts trained in greed—children of a curse!
Leaving the straight way, they have gone astray and followed the way of Balaam son of Bosor, who loved the wages of wrongdoing
verse.note: In the Old Testament Balaam’s father is named Beor (Numbers 22:5), and some manuscripts and many English versions have that name here. The best-attested reading is “Bosor,” a form not found elsewhere; its origin is uncertain, and it may reflect a variant pronunciation or a play on the Hebrew word for “flesh.”

verse.text: but was rebuked for his own lawbreaking: a voiceless donkey, speaking with a human voice, restrained the prophet’s madness.
These people are waterless springs and mists driven by a storm; for them the gloom of darkness has been kept.
For, speaking inflated, empty words, they lure with the desires of the flesh, with debauchery, people who are only just escaping from those who live in error.
They promise them freedom, though they themselves are slaves of corruption; for people are enslaved to whatever has defeated them.

For if, after escaping the defilements of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and defeated, their last state has become worse than the first.
For it would have been better for them not to have come to know the way of righteousness than, having come to know it, to turn back from the holy commandment handed on to them.
What the true proverb says has happened to them: “A dog returns to its own vomit,” and, “A sow, once washed, goes back to wallowing in the mud.”

note.term: “A dog returns to its own vomit,”

verse.note: The first saying is a loose form of Proverbs 26:11. The second is not from Scripture; it is often compared with a saying in the ancient Story of Ahiqar, and it appears to have been a common proverb. Dogs and pigs were both regarded as unclean animals, which sharpens the insult.

verse.text: This is now the second letter I am writing to you, dear friends. In both of them I am stirring up your sincere minds by way of reminder,
verse.note: The Greek word means “loved ones” and was an ordinary warm form of address. “Beloved” is the traditional rendering and is still used by several modern versions, but as a form of address it now sounds archaic. The same word is rendered “dear” of Paul in verse 15.

verse.text: so that you remember the words spoken beforehand by the holy prophets and the command of the Lord and Savior given through your apostles.
First of all, know this: in the last days mockers will come with their mockery, following their own desires
and saying, “Where is the promise of his coming? For from the day the fathers fell asleep, everything continues just as it has from the beginning of creation.”
verse.note: The Greek word means both arrival and presence, and was the regular term for the official visit of a king or emperor to a city. Christians used it for the expected return of Jesus. The same word is used in verse 12 of the arrival of “the day of God.”

This may mean the ancestors of Israel, as “the fathers” usually does in the New Testament, or the first generation of Christians, who had died without seeing the promised coming. Scholars are divided. The mockers’ appeal to “the beginning of creation” fits the first; the complaint about a delayed promise fits the second.

verse.text: For they deliberately let this escape them: that heavens existed long ago, and an earth formed out of water and through water by the word of God,

note.term: they deliberately let this escape them
note.traditional: they willingly are ignorant of / they deliberately overlook this fact

verse.note: The Greek can also be read “for in maintaining this, it escapes them that…,” where “this” is the mockers’ claim in verse 4. Most translations take it as deliberate ignorance, as here. The same verb “escape” returns in verse 8, where the readers are told not to make the mockers’ mistake.

The Greek is plural throughout this chapter and refers to the created heavens paired with the earth, not specifically to God’s dwelling. The plural is kept, as most English versions do here, because “heaven” would suggest God’s dwelling and “sky” would be too narrow for a passage about the whole created order. The phrase echoes “the heavens and the earth” of Genesis 1.

verse.text: and by these the world of that time was deluged with water and perished.
verse.note: The Greek pronoun is plural, and what it refers to is disputed. It may mean the waters (the earth was formed “out of water and through water” in verse 5, recalling Genesis 1), or water and God’s word together, or the heavens and the earth. In any case the allusion is to the flood of Genesis 6–8.

verse.text: But the present heavens and earth, by the same word, have been stored up for fire, kept for the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly people.
But do not let this one thing escape you, dear friends: with the Lord one day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years like one day.

note.term: one day is like a thousand years

verse.note: This draws on Psalm 90:4, “a thousand years in your sight are like yesterday when it is past.” The point is that God’s timescale is not the human one, so what looks like delay is not delay.

verse.text: The Lord is not slow about his promise, as some consider slowness, but is patient toward you, not wanting any to perish but all to come to turning back.
verse.note: “Repentance” now suggests mainly feeling sorry. The Greek word, shaped by the prophets’ call to “return” to God, means a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep “repentance” as an established term that readers understand to include a change of life.

verse.text: But the day of the Lord will come like a thief. On that day the heavens will pass away with a roar, the elements will be dissolved in the heat, and the earth and the works done on it will be found out.
verse.note: The Greek word could mean the basic materials of the physical world (earth, air, fire, water) or the heavenly bodies (sun, moon, and stars). Both senses are attested in the period, and scholars are divided. Because the word stands between “the heavens” and “the earth,” many favor the heavenly bodies.

The earliest manuscripts read “will be found,” which is difficult and is replaced in later manuscripts by “will be burned up” (so the King James Version), “will vanish,” and other readings. Most editors accept “will be found” as original and take it to mean exposed to God’s judgment; modern versions render it “laid bare,” “exposed,” or “disclosed.” The same verb recurs in verse 14, “to be found by him spotless.”

verse.text: Since all these things are to be dissolved in this way, what kind of people you ought to be, living in holy conduct and godliness,
waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God, because of which the heavens will be set on fire and dissolved, and the elements will melt in the heat!
verse.note: The verb can mean “to hurry something along” or “to be eager for, strive toward.” The first, adopted here and by most modern translations, implies that the readers’ way of life can bring the day nearer, an idea found in Jewish writings of the period. The second would give “waiting for and eagerly desiring the coming.”

verse.text: But according to his promise we wait for new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells.
Therefore, dear friends, since you are waiting for these things, make every effort to be found by him spotless and blameless, in peace,
and consider our Lord’s patience to be salvation, just as our dear brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given to him,

as he does in all his letters when he speaks in them about these things. In them are some things hard to understand, which the untaught and unstable twist, as they do the rest of the Scriptures, to their own destruction.
verse.note: The Greek word can mean simply “writings,” but in the New Testament it regularly means the sacred Scriptures. The phrase places Paul’s letters alongside them. It is one of the earliest indications that a collection of Paul’s letters was circulating and being read as authoritative.

verse.text: You therefore, dear friends, knowing this beforehand, be on your guard, so that you are not carried away by the error of the lawless and fall from your own stability.
But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.
verse.note: The Greek phrase, literally “to the day of the age,” occurs only here in the New Testament. It is not the usual idiom for “forever.” It probably means the day on which the age to come dawns, picking up the chapter’s theme of “the day of the Lord,” though some take it as eternity itself pictured as a single unending day.
